stories.teaser: A lizard dropped its tail 99 million years ago, and amber kept it
stories.headline: Tel Aviv University researchers find a 99-million-year-old lizard tail in amber, shed to escape danger
stories.why: Published in Palaeontologia Electronica; evidence the survival trick already existed 99 million years ago.
texts:
The oldest escape trick in the book.

Tel Aviv University researcher Dolev Fabrikant and colleagues studied a lizard tail preserved in amber about 99 million years old. Micro-CT scans showed a ring of muscle at the break, the same pattern living lizards form when they deliberately drop their tails. Published in Palaeontologia Electronica.

#Israel #TelAvivUniversity #Fossils #Science

Lizards were already dropping their tails in the age of the dinosaurs.

A 99-million-year-old amber specimen, now in the Steinhardt Museum of Natural History at Tel Aviv University, preserves a detached lizard tail with skin and muscle. The researchers say genes involved in tail regeneration may have arisen by at least 99 million years ago.

#Israel #TelAvivUniversity #Fossils #Science

Did it escape, or did a predator lose its meal?

Either way, a lizard tail landed in sticky tree resin about 99 million years ago. Tel Aviv University researchers scanned the amber and found the telltale muscle pattern of a deliberate tail drop, documenting a behavior, not just an anatomy, from the mid-Cretaceous.

#Israel #TelAvivUniversity #Fossils #Science
stories.og_title: Lizard Dropped Its Tail 99 Million Years Ago, Amber Preserved Evidence

stories.teaser: Why our knees wear out: the trade-off behind the human brain
stories.headline: Weizmann Institute study in Nature links our flexible brains to our fragile knees
stories.why: A genome-wide study with Kyoto University points to a molecule behind both, and possible new osteoarthritis research.
texts:
Smart brains, weak knees.

Weizmann Institute researchers led by Dr. David Gokhman, with Kyoto University, found that humans make fewer GAGs, shock-absorbing molecules in joint cartilage that also stiffen brain connections. The result: flexible brains, but joints less able to absorb shocks. Published in Nature.

“We have a unique brain with high capabilities, but our fragile skeleton goes through degeneration very fast.”

#Israel #Weizmann #Evolution #Science

About 500,000 single-letter DNA differences separate humans from chimpanzees.

Weizmann Institute and Kyoto University scientists searched them for the ones that changed skeletal development, and found a gene group that is strongly silenced in humans. Published in Nature, the study could point toward new research on osteoarthritis, which affects hundreds of millions of people.

#Israel #Weizmann #Evolution #Science

“We can see step by step what evolution did, and we can also see diseases that emerged in our evolution,” says Dr. David Gokhman of the Weizmann Institute.

His team found that the same change that helps keep human brains flexible may also have made our joints less effective at absorbing shocks. The study was published in Nature.

#Israel #Weizmann #Evolution #Science
stories.og_title: Weak knees, smart brains: Israeli study gets to the bottom of genetic evolution

stories.teaser: Can crowds predict the future? A million forecasts say: pretty well
stories.headline: Tel Aviv University study of over a million forecasts finds crowds predict the future surprisingly well
stories.why: Published in PNAS; analyzed forecasts from four prediction platforms across 12 domains.
texts:
Can we really predict the future?

Tel Aviv University researchers led by Prof. Michael Gilead analyzed 1,014,122 forecasts from four prediction platforms, covering a decade of elections, technology, geopolitics and more. Crowd forecasts matched reality well: events given a 70% chance happened about 70% of the time. Published in PNAS.

#Israel #TelAvivUniversity #Psychology #Science

Events given a 70% chance of happening occurred approximately 70% of the time.

That’s what Tel Aviv University psychologists found after studying over a million crowd forecasts from Polymarket, Kalshi, Manifold and Metaculus. Forecasts were already well calibrated after just 25% of their forecasting period. The researchers stress this doesn’t mean anyone can predict the future with certainty.

#Israel #TelAvivUniversity #Psychology #Science

A million predictions, put to the test.

Prof. Michael Gilead’s team at Tel Aviv University checked forecasts across 12 domains against what actually happened. Crowds were well calibrated overall, though they tended to overestimate events in technology and international relations and underestimate election-related ones. The study was published in PNAS.

#Israel #TelAvivUniversity #Psychology #Science
stories.og_title: Can We Really Predict the Future?

stories.teaser: Six Israeli researchers join Cornell through a new exchange
stories.headline: Cornell launches an Israeli scholar exchange, welcoming six researchers from Jewish and Arab communities
stories.why: The Kalaniyot chapter at Cornell hosts Israeli postdocs and sabbatical scholars in fields from gut health to quantum computing.
texts:
Six Israeli scientists, one American campus.

Cornell University launched a Kalaniyot chapter, hosting three postdoctoral fellows and three sabbatical scholars from Israel’s Jewish and Arab communities. Their work ranges from gut health and wetlands to detecting plant disease and trapped-ion quantum computing.

“Anyone with a Ph.D. from an Israeli university, or a faculty position at one, can apply.”

#Israel #Cornell #Science #Kalaniyot

From ponds to quantum sensors.

Israeli hydrologist Ohad Shalom is studying ponds and wetlands at Cornell. Loai Basheer is looking at how the spotted lanternfly affects grape products, and Ori Katz is working on trapped-ion quantum computing. They are part of the first cohort of Cornell’s new Kalaniyot chapter for Israeli scholars.

#Israel #Cornell #Science #Kalaniyot

Science keeps building bridges.

Cornell’s new Kalaniyot chapter, one of seven in the US, brings Israeli researchers to campus. Its first six scholars, from both Jewish and Arab communities, are working with Cornell faculty on nutrition, ecology, plant disease, developmental science and quantum physics. Cornell said religion and ethnicity are not considered in selection.

#Israel #Cornell #Science #Kalaniyot
stories.og_title: Cornell launches Israeli scholar exchange with six researchers on campus
